identity.title: The Element Isn't the Whole Story
identity.description: Two <input> elements can behave completely differently depending on nothing but an attribute. This lesson is about the difference between what an element IS and how it's CONFIGURED — and why that distinction matters every time you write markup.

primaryCapability.statement: Configure an HTML element's behavior using attributes, and distinguish the element itself from its configuration.

knows: HTML documents are trees of nested elements
Elements are written with opening and closing tags
canDo: Read and construct simple nested markup
likelyMisconceptions: Attributes are decoration, similar to styling
Any attribute can be added to any element and the browser will just ignore what doesn't apply

canDo: Explain the difference between an element and its attributes
Predict how changing an attribute changes browser behavior
Choose an appropriate attribute for a given element and purpose

learning.targetMentalModel: An element is a kind of thing (a link, an input, an image). An attribute configures that specific instance of it. The same element type can behave very differently depending on its attributes — and not every attribute is meaningful on every element.

experience.startingState: The learner can read nesting but has been treating tags as fixed, self-contained units.
experience.narrativeContext: The same tag name is shown behaving in two different ways to force the element/attribute distinction into view.
experience.primaryInteraction: Predicting behavior from attributes, then configuring an element correctly, then reasoning about which attribute fits a scenario.
experience.expectedOutcome: The learner treats every element as "tag + its configuration" by default.

activities.title: The Element Isn't the Whole Story

content.title: The Element Isn't the Whole Story
content.hook:
<input type="checkbox">
<input type="text">

Both of these are <input> elements. One renders as a little box you click. The other renders as a text field. Same tag name — completely different behavior.
content.context: The difference lives entirely in one word: type="...". That word is an attribute, and attributes are what this lesson is about.
goals: Distinguish an element from its configuration
Read and use attribute syntax correctly

content.title: Name, Value, Configuration
content.text:
An attribute lives inside an element's opening tag, written as name="value". <a href="/about"> has one attribute: href, with the value "/about". The element (<a>, a link) stays the same kind of thing no matter what href you give it — but href is what tells the browser where that specific link actually goes. Change the value, and the link's destination changes. Remove it entirely, and you have a link that goes nowhere.

Attributes configure a specific instance of an element. They don't change what kind of element it is.
content.keyTakeaway: Element = what kind of thing. Attribute = how this specific one is configured.

activities.title: Predict the Behavior
activities.instruction:
<input type="checkbox" checked>

What will this render as when the page loads?

options.text: A text field containing the word "checked"

hints.text: type="checkbox" already tells you what kind of input this is. What might a second, separate word right after it be doing?
"checked" isn't inside quotes attached to another attribute — it's its own attribute, present on its own.

activities.title: Configure a Real Link
activities.instruction: Complete the <a> element so it links to "https://developer.mozilla.org" and opens in a new tab. Opening in a new tab requires the attribute target with the value "_blank".

hints.text: Attributes go inside the opening tag, after the tag name, separated by spaces.
You need two attributes on the same <a> tag: href and target.
Read the docs — fill in both values.

activities.title: Not Every Attribute Belongs Everywhere
activities.instruction: You're marking up a <button> that submits a form. A teammate suggests adding an href attribute to it "just in case it's useful." What's the right call?

content.scenario: A <button type="submit"> inside a form. A teammate wants to add href="#" to it, reasoning that it might be handy for styling hooks later.

options.text: Don't add it — href isn't a meaningful attribute on <button>; it belongs on <a>, and adding it won't do anything useful.
Add it — extra attributes never cause problems, so there's no real downside.
Add it, then use the href value directly in the button's click handler.

content.title: What You Can Do Now
takeaways: An attribute is a name="value" pair inside an opening tag that configures that specific element instance.
The same element type can behave very differently depending on its attributes.
Not every attribute is meaningful on every element — attributes belong to the elements that actually use them.
nextSteps: Next: using headings to structure a document, not just to make text bigger.
